summary: Introduces extensions to Mobile IPv6 and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for handling local mobility. A Mobility Anchor Point reduces the signaling between a moving device, its correspondents and its home agent. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 5380.

eli5.summary: When you move around inside a big building, a front desk can forward your mail so far-away friends do not need your new room each time. The anchor point acts like that front desk for moving devices.

questions: what is a mobility anchor point
what is a regional care-of address
subtitle: A local anchor point reduces signaling when devices move within a domain.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 requires a moving device to send binding updates to every correspondent node and its home agent. This creates delay and bandwidth overhead, especially over wireless links.
tldr.mechanism: A Mobility Anchor Point (MAP) acts as a local home agent within a visited network. The mobile node registers only with the MAP, which forwards packets to the device's current address. The MAP's address stays constant within its domain.
tldr.outcome: Signaling outside the local domain is reduced, and handover speed improves. However, the design is experimental and was superseded by RFC 5380, which uses more modern mobility concepts.

facts.label: Signaling reduction
facts.value: One binding update per move instead of one per correspondent

today: RFC 4140 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 5380, which defines a more modern approach to hierarchical mobile IPv6.

sections.title: Hierarchical Mobility and the Mobility Anchor Point
sections.content:
RFC 4140 extends Mobile IPv6 by introducing the Mobility Anchor Point (MAP), a router that acts as a local home agent within a visited network. When a mobile node enters a MAP domain, it registers with the MAP instead of sending binding updates to every peer and its distant home agent.

The traditional Mobile IPv6 approach requires a mobile node to send binding updates to its home agent and every correspondent node whenever it moves. Each update must pass return-routability checks, taking 1.5 round-trip times per correspondent node. This overhead disrupts active connections during handovers. The MAP solves this by becoming the anchor point for a local domain.
sections.eli5: Instead of telling everyone new information every time you move, you tell one person and they handle it for you.

sections.title: Regional and On-Link Care-of Addresses
sections.content:
HMIPv6 introduces two types of care-of addresses. The Regional Care-of Address (RCoA) is an address on the MAP's subnet that the mobile node uses with its home agent and correspondent nodes. The on-link Care-of Address (LCoA) is the mobile node's actual address on its current access link.

When the mobile node moves within a MAP domain, only the LCoA changes; the RCoA remains constant. This makes mobility transparent to correspondent nodes and the home agent. The mobile node registers bindings with the MAP using both addresses, and the MAP maintains a binding cache mapping the RCoA to the current LCoA.
sections.eli5: The postal address (RCoA) stays the same, but your actual location (LCoA) can change. The MAP knows both and forwards mail to your real location.

sections.title: Protocol Operation and Binding Updates
sections.content:
The mobile node performs a Local Binding Update to the MAP by sending a binding update with the M flag set, specifying its RCoA and LCoA. The MAP responds with a binding acknowledgement and performs Duplicate Address Detection on the RCoA. A bidirectional tunnel is established between the mobile node and MAP.

Packets sent by the mobile node are tunneled to the MAP with the LCoA as the source and MAP address as the destination. Incoming packets addressed to the RCoA are intercepted by the MAP and tunneled to the LCoA. After registering with the MAP, the mobile node sends its RCoA to the home agent and correspondent nodes as it would in standard Mobile IPv6.
sections.eli5: You send a message to the front desk with your room number. From then on, incoming mail gets tunneled to your real location, and outgoing mail goes through the desk first.

sections.title: MAP Discovery and Selection
sections.content:
Mobile nodes discover MAPs through Router Advertisements containing a new MAP option. The option includes the MAP's address, a distance metric reflecting its proximity, a preference value, and a valid lifetime. The distance field helps mobile nodes choose between multiple MAPs; a higher distance suggests the MAP is further up in the hierarchy.

An HMIPv6-aware mobile node selects a MAP based on preference and distance. The RFC recommends selecting the most distant MAP with non-zero preference, as this reduces the frequency of MAP changes for fast-moving nodes. If the MAP option includes a valid lifetime of zero, the mobile node treats it as a MAP failure and selects another MAP or falls back to standard Mobile IPv6.
sections.eli5: Router advertisements tell you which front desks are available, how far they are, and how good they are. You pick the best one.

sections.title: Security Between Mobile Node and MAP
sections.content:
The security relationship between the mobile node and MAP must be strong. The RFC mandates mutual authentication, integrity protection, and replay attack protection. IKE can establish a Security Association for the RCoA without requiring the mobile node to prove ownership of the RCoA before the first binding update, unlike standard Mobile IPv6.

Binding updates between the mobile node and MAP must be protected with AH or ESP in transport mode. The MAP does not need prior knowledge of the mobile node's identity or home address, simplifying the security setup. However, the RFC notes that if a binding cache entry exists for an RCoA, the MAP must ensure that new binding updates come from the same mobile node that established the original association.
sections.eli5: You and the front desk need a secret handshake so you know you're talking to the real desk, not an impostor.
